Ba_al.json.text:
Ba'al is a non-Celtic divinity. The title means "the lord." The Phoenicians used it for several of their gods. This ancient people traded across the eastern Mediterranean. Ba'al was parallel to the goddess Ba'alat. Her title means "the lady." Ba'al may have served as her consort.

Writers sometimes mistake Ba'al for Celtic. They tie him to a supposed god named Bel. Bel was said to give its name to Beltane, the May Day feast. No evidence supports Bel. No inscriptions or statues of Bel survive. A god named Belenus does appear in the record. His name may sit inside the festival name. Belenus differs from Ba'al in role. Ba'al ruled the atmosphere, especially in stormy weather. Belenus governed healing springs and, at times, the sun.

okr.objective: Describe Ba'al as a non-Celtic Phoenician title, not the god Bel.
key_results: The title Ba'al means the lord and applied to several Phoenician gods.
Ba'al was parallel to, and possible consort of, the goddess Ba'alat.
The god Bel has no inscriptions or statues to prove his existence.
Belenus, linked to healing springs, is a separate god from Ba'al.
okr.evidence: Monaghan, Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore

Barinthus.json.text:
Barinthus is an Arthurian hero. The texts also call him Saint Barrind. He served as the ferryman of the Otherworld. His task was to carry journeys between realms.

His great duty came at the end of King Arthur's story. Arthur fought a final battle and was wounded. Barinthus then carried the wounded king away. He took Arthur from the surface world to the Otherworld. The act seals Barinthus as a liminal guide between the living world and the supernatural land.

Barrax.json.text:
Barrax is an obscure British god. The record lists him under the forms Barrecis and Barrex. He is known from a single dedication only. The occupying Roman armies likened him to their god of war, Mars.

The name carries a concrete meaning. Barrax in the Celtic tongue seems to mean "supreme" or "lordly." This sparse record leaves little else. Only one inscription witnesses his worship. He remains one of the faintest British gods.

Bath.json.text:
Bath is a British mythological site. It lies in the southwest of England. Great hot springs bubble from the earth there. The waters have been prized for healing for at least two thousand years. Some think the spring was used before the Celts. The records that survive date from Celtic times. The Romans named the town Aquae Sulis.

The Celts linked the site to their goddess Sul. The Romans folded Sul into their goddess Minerva. They built colonnaded temples and interior bathing rooms. These buildings stand today.

Celtic custom showed itself at Bath. People threw coins into the water. They also wrote curses on sheets of lead. Excavators have found 16,000 coins at the site. They have found more than 50 cursing tablets as well.

Baudwin.json.text:
Baudwin is an Arthurian hero. The texts also call him Baudwin of Brittany. He was one of the few knights to survive the brutal battle of Camlan. This battle came near the end of King Arthur's reign.

After the battle, Baudwin changed his life. He chose to live as a hermit. His survival and retreat mark a quiet end to a knight's career.

Beare.json.text:
Beare is an Irish goddess. She gave her name to a peninsula in the far southwest of Ireland. The land lies in the province of Munster. The thin Beare peninsula stretches out to sea. It is rich in both antiquities and legend.

Beare is also called Bera, Béirre, or Moméa. Little of her own legend survives. She is said to have been a Spanish princess. The greater fame belongs to the Cailleach Bhéirre, the Hag of Beare. She was an ancient land goddess of the pre-Celtic people.

The Hag stays bound to the peninsula. A boulder in her shape looks toward the sea from the north side. In some tellings the consonants shift. Then her name becomes Moméa.

Bebo.json.text:
Bebo is an Irish heroine. She was the small wife of the tiny fairy king Iubdán. She traveled with this husband to the land of Ulster. The region seemed full of giants to the pair. The lovely queen caught the eye of the Ulster king, Fergus.

Bebo became Fergus's mistress for a year. The bond held despite the great physical difference. Fergus then gave Bebo back. Her husband offered him a pair of magical shoes. The enchanted pair sealed the exchange.

Bec.json.text:
Bec is an Irish hero. The name means "small." Several figures in Irish legend bear this title. Each is a minor hero of the cycle.

One is Bec mac Buain. He was the father of the maidens who guarded a magical well. The hero Fionn Mac Cumhaill gained wisdom there. A girl accidentally spilled some water into his mouth. The spill passed on the well's power.

Another is Bec mac Bé, a diviner. His skill let him answer nine questions in a single reply. One answer settled all nine at once.
